column1: # nearby-probes.tsv — what `Index::nearby` answers, for every reader of the .vst extract to
# check itself against. Rust, Dart, Swift and Kotlin assert against this file rather than
# against each other: four readings of one ordering is four chances to drift.
# Regenerate (needs Postgres; this file is the output):
#   cd backend && cargo test --release --lib write_the_nearby_probe_fixture -- --ignored --nocapture
# Columns, tab separated:
#   lat  lon  limit  search_radius_m  complete  ids  label
# `complete` is 1 or 0 — it is `!hits.is_empty()`, which the umbrella sizing fails closed on.
# `search_radius_m` is the wire spelling (`handlers.rs`); `searched_radius_m` is only the Rust
# struct's field name. `ids` are bare record ids in the answer's order, comma separated and
# empty when nothing is near — the wire's `vs:` prefix has no business in a fixture. `label`
# is for whoever reads a failure, and is never asserted on.
# No row is marked `ambiguous`, deliberately. A tie looks like it would need that, but both
# of `Index::nearby`'s sorts are stable and the extract's records ascend by id, so two
# stations at the same rounded metre resolve the same way in every language. Marking rows
# lenient that are in fact determined would only hide a real divergence.
# Coordinates are on the micro-degree grid — the grid the extract stores — and every answer
# was computed from exactly the value printed here. Parse the coordinate back and you hold
# the bit-identical input, so no reader can diverge through rounding.
# The line below names the extract these answers belong to. Both numbers are a pure function
# of the table — the CRC covers [header_len, EOF), so neither moves when the import serial or
# the generated timestamp does. A fixture for another import is not a looser assertion, it is
# a wrong one.
# crc32=0xb04add01 count=7604
